proposals.name: Repairs the asker's own attempt at its exact break point
proposals.instruction: Score how precisely the answer locates and mends the asker's specific work. 10: the answer names the exact line, step, sign, or quantity in the asker's attempt that fails, states the correction using the asker's own variables and notation, and says explicitly what was already correct so the asker knows where to resume. 8-9: clearly engages the asker's attempt and localizes the trouble, though slightly less surgically. 4-6: acknowledges the asker's approach in general terms but does not pinpoint anything. 1-3: mentions the asker only in passing. 0: a free-standing exposition that could have been written without ever reading the asker's attempt.
proposals.rationale: The largest single family among the items the dense model ranks high. R60 opens by certifying the asker's method and then names the one line where signs went wrong; R45 identifies exactly which factor is missing from the asker's numerator terms; R40 continues from the asker's own substitution ('If, as you did, w = e^{iz}'); R23 begins 'Your DFA looks good to me'; R36 diagnoses which two concepts the asker has fused. A scorecard reading for correctness and completeness scores the mathematics of these as thin (R60 supplies one corrected line, R45 no formula at all), so it lands them low, while the dense model reads the tight coupling to the asker's text.

proposals.name: Deliberate handover: leaves a clean, achievable last step
proposals.instruction: Score how well the answer stops at the right place and marks the handover. 10: it advances the problem until only mechanical work remains, states plainly that this remainder is the reader's ('I leave it to you to simplify', 'now you have two equations and two unknowns'), and has supplied enough that the remainder is genuinely achievable. 6-8: stops short with adequate scaffolding but does not signal the handover. 3-5: carries out the routine remainder in full even though it adds nothing. 0-2: either grinds every trivial step to the final numeral, or stops so early the reader has been given no usable purchase at all.
proposals.rationale: Directly opposes the completeness pressure a criterion bank applies. R19 derives the summation and then writes 'I leave it you to simplify this expression'; R57 works three digits of the expansion and hands over 'now you have to figure out when it becomes periodic'; R35 sets up the pair of equations and stops; R32 gives a three-rung ladder of lemmas to prove; R37 asks 'Can you think of an x1 and x2 that meet these requirements?'. All sit high on the dense side with very low card percentiles, which is what an explicit completeness criterion would produce.

proposals.name: Names the unlocking idea in one or two lines
proposals.instruction: Score whether the answer isolates a single pivot that collapses the problem. 10: within the first sentence or two it names the specific substitution, identity, isomorphism, factorization, or reduction that makes the rest routine, stated precisely enough to act on immediately, and does not pad around it. 5-7: a pivot exists but is buried inside longer manipulation. 2-4: several partial ideas, none identified as the key. 0: an undifferentiated sequence of routine manipulations with no nameable turning point.
proposals.rationale: R17 is three lines long and consists entirely of the observation that the group is D6 plus a pointer; R43 is two lines, reducing to horizontal and vertical lines plus a citation; R08 gives only the partial-fraction split and the tangent substitution; R54 is a single sentence naming the Gamma integral with Euler's formula; R29 completes the square and states the answer. These are near the top for the dense model and near the bottom for the scorecard, because per-criterion scoring of a two-line answer has almost nothing to reward.

proposals.name: Stands alone rather than riding on sibling answers
proposals.instruction: Score how far the answer reads as a self-standing response rather than an addendum. 10: it could be the only answer on the page; it never names, praises, corrects, or positions itself against another answer to the same question, and its argument is complete without them. 5-7: a single passing nod to another answer, but the argument stands alone. 2-4: opens by referencing another answer and supplies mainly a delta on top of it. 0: the whole point of the text is supplementary ('a complementary note to X and Y', 'essentially the same as X but simplified', 'this second answer', 'another point of view'), so that removing the sibling answers would leave it incoherent.
proposals.rationale: This positioning marks almost half the items the dense model ranks low. R05 opens by calling another answer 'very good' and then covers only the leftover lemma; R20 announces itself as 'a complimentary note to MichaelNgelo and Sherushe's answers'; R47 opens '(Essentially the same as TheSilverDoe's but much simplified.)'; R04 begins 'Also note that'; R16 begins 'This second answer'; R56 begins 'Another point view'; R52 begins 'The argument that follows is probably a variant of what Qiaochu Yuan had in mind'. A criterion bank scores the mathematics inside these and finds it clean, so it ranks them very high, while the dense model registers that the text presents itself as a footnote.

proposals.name: Load-bearing step present in the text, not behind a link
proposals.instruction: Score self-containedness of the argument's core. 10: every step the argument depends on appears in the answer itself; any external reference is provenance, orientation, or further reading, and the reader can finish without following it. 6-8: minor supporting facts are cited outward but the spine is present. 3-5: an important intermediate result is asserted by reference. 0: the central derivation is delegated ('as shown in this post', 'in this answer it is shown that'), so a reader who does not chase the pointer gets nothing.
proposals.rationale: Distinguishable from A04 and worth separating, because outward citation is not uniformly a defect. R09 hands its whole solution formula to another post and only differentiates afterwards; R05 outsources the integrality lemma the same way; R11 leans on 'as mentioned before' and 'as in my post' for both generating-function identities. Contrast R43 and R44, which cite a Monthly paper and a Wikipedia figure respectively yet state inline exactly what to take from them; both sit high on the dense side. A criterion bank checking whether steps are justified will accept a citation as justification and misses the difference.

proposals.name: Prose mechanics and typographic hygiene
proposals.instruction: Score surface craft only, independent of mathematical merit. 10: clean sentences, correct spelling and homophones, spaces after punctuation, consistent use of mathematical typesetting throughout, symbols rendered the same way in every occurrence. 6-8: one or two blemishes. 3-5: repeated typos, run-together punctuation, or mathematics typed as plain text in an answer that elsewhere typesets it. 0: pervasive misspellings and homophone errors, missing spaces, mixed plain-text and typeset notation, so the reader must decode the surface before reaching the argument.
proposals.rationale: Cheap to judge and invisible to a bank aimed at mathematical properties. R13 writes 'than' for 'then' twice inside a short argument and is cramped throughout; R24 runs sentences together ('You mixed them up.If you look') and drops spaces before commas; R12 mixes plain-text arrows and inequalities into an otherwise prose argument; R56 repeats the non-English 'simple objets' and opens 'Another point view towards'. All four are ranked low by the dense model and high by the scorecard, which is exactly the pattern if the bank never asks about surface quality.

proposals.name: Payload per line, penalizing digressive self-commentary
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the text is doing work. 10: nothing could be cut without losing content; length is set by the problem, not by the writer's momentum. 6-8: mostly efficient with some redundancy. 3-5: noticeably padded, restating the same move in several registers. 0-2: long and meandering, with repeated restarts, and closing meta-commentary about the writing itself or about what the asker may already know, none of which advances the mathematics.
proposals.rationale: The scorecard appears to reward bulk, since long items cluster at its top. R12 runs many paragraphs and closes with two notes, one conceding 'I am not 100% sure that you weren't aware of all that already' and another second-guessing whether the demonstration is elegant; R41 sets homework mid-answer and restates the same intuition repeatedly; R20 and R18 spell out routine chases at length. Against them, R17, R43, and R54 are one to three lines and sit near the top for the dense model. Length is doing the work in the bank's ranking and the opposite in the dense model's.

proposals.name: Works inside the asker's demonstrated framework and notation
proposals.instruction: Score register match. 10: the answer uses the objects, notation, and machinery the question itself displays, and any new tool is introduced only after being motivated and briefly explained. 6-8: modestly heavier than the question but bridged. 3-5: reframes the problem in apparatus the asker has plainly not met, without a bridge. 0: explicitly discards the asker's setting or ideas and substitutes an unrelated and heavier framework, leaving the asker no route from what they wrote to what is written back.
proposals.rationale: R16 states outright that it 'does not expand on your ideas' and proceeds through equivariance, constant rank, and stabilizers; R26 answers a Munkres exercise with T4 spaces and the Aleksandrov compactification in a single dense paragraph; R22 lifts a finite matrix question into an infinite matrix and Moebius inversion; R10 concedes the asker asked for a non-graph route and supplies a graph route anyway. All are ranked high by the scorecard, which will read them as rigorous and general, and low by the dense model. The contrast cases R40 and R03 stay entirely inside the asker's own objects.

proposals.name: Delivers what was asked, honoring stated constraints
proposals.instruction: Score fit between what the question requests and what the text supplies. 10: it produces the requested object under the constraints the question states, and where it declines a constraint it says why and still leaves the asker a usable path. 6-8: on target with minor drift. 3-5: answers a nearby question the writer preferred. 0: contradicts an explicit constraint in the question, or disposes of the question by denying its premise while leaving the asker nothing to do next.
proposals.rationale: R10 opens 'I know that you ask about non-graph approaches in particular' and then gives the graph argument regardless; R25 dispatches the question by observing the equation has no solutions, with no path forward for the asker; R56 substitutes general remarks about simple objects for the requested intuition. Each is high on the scorecard, which can only see a correct and well-organized piece of mathematics. R01 shows the other side: it answers the question the asker actually had rather than the one literally typed.

proposals.name: Candor about the mathematics versus deference about standing
proposals.instruction: Composite. Score both the presence of honest epistemic marking about the argument and the absence of status-hedging about the writer. 10: the answer flags a real limitation, gap, or outright failure in its own reasoning in plain terms ('this is broken', 'I am not sure this solves the problem, there may be an error elsewhere'), while still owning the answer and offering the better route. 5-7: no epistemic marking where none is needed. 2-4: unmarked hedging that is really about the writer's position. 0: the hedge concerns the writer's standing relative to other answerers or the asker ('probably a variant of what X had in mind', 'I think I have the answer', 'I am not sure you weren't already aware of this'), with no acknowledgement of any actual gap in the mathematics.
proposals.rationale: The two hedge types point in opposite directions across the slice, which a single 'confidence' or 'hedging' criterion would blur. Candid about the math and ranked high by the dense model: R49 posts a slick manipulation then appends 'edit: And well, this is broken'; R28 says 'I'm not sure if that solves the problem, there might be an error elsewhere' and then gives the cleaner route; R23 offers three suggestions 'and no promise that they will be helpful'. Deferential about standing and ranked low: R52, R11, and R12's closing note. A bank is likely to treat all hedging as one property.

proposals.name: Dissolves the confusion behind the question
proposals.instruction: Score whether the answer treats the cause of the asker's difficulty. 10: it identifies the misconception, hidden convention, or apparent paradox that generated the question and removes it, so the asker sees why they were stuck. 6-8: addresses the stated question well and gestures at the underlying issue. 3-5: executes the requested computation competently without touching why the asker was confused. 0: restates standard material with no diagnostic content whatsoever.
proposals.rationale: The slice contains a controlled pair on the same question. R01 and R21 both address the range of an inverse-cotangent composition; R21 grinds the composition to the interval and is ranked high by the scorecard and low by the dense model, while R01 explains that a computer algebra system uses a different branch convention, which is what made the asker's result look wrong, and is ranked the other way around. R36 ('You seem to be greatly confused on a couple of concepts') and R59 (quoting the asker's definition back and answering 'Nope!') show the same diagnostic move. A completeness-and-correctness bank cannot distinguish the pair, since R21 is more complete.

proposals.name: Warns about the next trap, not just the present one
proposals.instruction: Score forward guardrails. 10: after resolving the immediate issue the answer flags the boundary, side condition, or second error the reader is about to hit, concretely enough to be recognized when it arrives. 6-8: some caveat is offered. 3-5: notes a limitation only vaguely. 0: closes at the first resolution with no indication of where the reasoning stops being safe.
proposals.rationale: A distinctly expert habit that adds no rigor a criterion bank would score. R45 fixes the missing multiplier and then warns 'This still won't quite do it, because your method isn't counting scenarios like two pairs of people each of whom have the same birthday'; R58 answers the yes-or-no question and immediately bounds it with the region-of-convergence caveat and a parallel example; R46 offers an intuition and simultaneously labels it 'rather dangerous'; R01 notes the workaround is 'not ideal in cases where we want a continuous function' before giving it. All four are ranked well above their scorecard percentile.

proposals.name: Runs the general procedure on a concrete numerical instance
proposals.instruction: Score concreteness of instantiation. 10: the general method is executed on a specific small instance with actual numbers, with the intermediate state displayed after each step so the reader can follow the state changing. 6-8: an example is given but only partially worked. 3-5: an example is mentioned but not carried out. 0: purely symbolic throughout, with no instance the reader can check against.
proposals.rationale: R03 states the elimination rule and then performs it on a specific three-by-three matrix, printing both factors after every single update, and is one of the sharpest disagreements in the slice; R57 does the same for a decimal expansion, showing each digit emerge from an explicit division; R19 counts a concrete configuration of balls in words before writing the sum. A bank scoring rigor, generality, or justification will treat a worked instance as adding nothing, since the general statement was already present.

proposals.name: Displayed material is legible, necessary, and internally consistent
proposals.instruction: Composite. Score whether the reader can actually see the object being argued about. 10: every large display is introduced, is needed for the argument, is small enough to read, and its entries are consistent with the pattern it claims; where the argument is geometric, the figure is supplied, pointed to concretely, or the configuration is reconstructible from the text; a final result, if there is one, is easy to find. 5-7: displays are heavy but survivable and consistent. 2-4: a page-sized array that mostly restates a standard formula, or a configuration of many labelled points with no figure and no reconstruction. 0: both, or a display whose entries visibly contradict the pattern it is presented as following.
proposals.rationale: Bulk of typeset material appears to attract the scorecard while the dense model reads legibility. R02 devotes most of its height to a full cofactor array whose blocks do not all follow the stated minor pattern (the second row mixes indices in a way inconsistent with the first), and the array is only used to extract one entry; R34 labels foci, tangency points, reflections, and two auxiliary directions across four bolded steps with no figure and no instruction to draw one. Both are near the scorecard's ceiling. The contrasting cases are R51, where an equally large display is the derivation itself with the result marked in colour, R27, where the highlighting tracks the case space visibly shrinking, and R44, which resolves the figure problem by pointing at specific existing pictures and saying what to do with them.

proposals.name: Written to a person: second-person diagnosis and encouragement
proposals.instruction: Score address and stance toward the reader. 10: written in the second person to the individual who asked, with a verdict on where they stand, a next action, and an encouraging or checking close ('keep doing what you're doing', 'does that make sense?'), including where relevant a frank opinion the writer owns. 6-8: some second-person address without the arc. 3-5: impersonal but readable exposition. 0: entirely impersonal, addressed to no one, reading as a lecture note or a proof transcript with no awareness that a specific person is on the other end.
proposals.rationale: Separable from A01, which is about locating a mathematical error; this is about stance, and it covers items where there was no error to locate. R55 explains the display, asks 'Does that make sense?', and then volunteers a frank opinion that the technique is obsolete and teaching it is 'kind of silly'; R60 closes with 'keep doing what you're doing'; R35 and R37 both end by handing the reader a next action in the second person; R23 and R19 are conversational throughout. The dense-low items are overwhelmingly impersonal by contrast, including R02, R18, R22, R42, and R52, none of which address anyone. A criterion bank built around properties of the mathematics has no reason to encode stance.

proposals.name: Sheer bulk: length, paragraph count, enumerated-step volume
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH TEXT AND HOW MANY DISCRETE STEPS the answer contains: total running length, number of paragraphs, number of separately displayed formula blocks, and number of enumerated or labelled stages of the development. 0 = one or two lines with at most one formula; 3 = a short paragraph plus a formula; 5 = a moderate multi-paragraph development; 8 = many paragraphs with many displayed blocks; 10 = a very long post with extended case analysis or many enumerated stages. Count volume only. Do NOT judge whether the length is appropriate, whether the extra material is useful, whether the post is thorough or padded, or whether any of it is correct.
proposals.rationale: MODE 1. Volume varies by more than an order of magnitude across the slice and in both disagreement directions: R34 and R13 run to screens of enumerated case analysis, R01 and R25 are long expositions, while R49 is two lines, R37 is a single hint sentence, R45 is a one-line citation and R21 is three lines. Length is countable without reading for merit, and both a text-only dense model and a many-criterion scorecard can accumulate score with bulk alone, so it is predictive without being about whether sibling answers' voters preferred this one. Tagged mixed because a larger effort budget may also genuinely produce a better answer.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's effort budget / chosen scope for the post

proposals.name: Subject-matter altitude: coursework topic versus graduate machinery
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW ADVANCED THE MATHEMATICAL SUBJECT MATTER IS, judged from vocabulary and named objects alone. 0 = elementary or early-undergraduate material (exponent rules, decimal expansion, stem-and-leaf plots, row reduction, basic counting); 3 = routine first-year calculus or linear algebra; 5 = standard mid-undergraduate (complex numbers, elementary number theory, series convergence); 8 = advanced undergraduate or first-year graduate (measure theory, topology, Galois theory); 10 = research-adjacent vocabulary (relative homology of pairs, Riemann surfaces and branch gluing, weak convergence in Hilbert space, scheme-theoretic language, structure theory of simple Lie algebras). Score the ALTITUDE of the vocabulary only. Do NOT judge whether the mathematics is done well, whether advanced material is impressive, whether the exposition suits the level, or whether anything is correct.
proposals.rationale: MODE 1 topic markers and MODE 4 kind-of-question. Elementary rows cluster on one side of the disagreement (R25 row reduction, R55 free variables, R32 stem-and-leaf, R33 exponent rules, R39 solving for two coefficients) and graduate rows on the other (R19 orbits of symmetric matrices, R29 relative homology, R13 Riemann surfaces, R47 weak convergence, R16 simple Lie groups). Tagged not-mixed on a structural argument: subject-matter altitude is essentially CONSTANT across the sibling answers to one question - R01 and R14 answer the same entropy question, R08 and R60 answer the same range-of-g question - so it cannot cause a within-question preference among siblings. Any predictive power it carries is a pure between-question level confound that a within-question target must not absorb.
proposals.upstream_parent: the kind of question the answer is attached to and which sub-audience it draws

proposals.name: Site-markup fluency versus plaintext ASCII mathematical orthography
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW FLUENTLY THE POST USES THE SITE'S MATHEMATICAL MARKUP. Raise the score for: consistent inline and display mathematics; aligned, align-star, cases, matrix and pmatrix environments; equation tags and numbered references to them; macro definitions introduced at the top of the post; structural markup such as bold step labels, lists and blockquotes; and idiomatic blackboard-bold and script symbol conventions. Lower the score when mathematics is written in plaintext or programming-style ASCII instead - for example '5^10 = 9,765,625', '3.68 x 10^-6', 'f(x) = a*x^{1/2} + bx', '1/2*a*x^{-1/2}', or products written with asterisks - or when formulas are simply run into prose untypeset. 0 = no markup at all; 5 = plain inline mathematics with a few displays; 10 = dense, idiomatic, multi-environment typesetting including macros or tags. Score only the EXTENT of markup fluency. Do NOT judge whether the typesetting is pretty, whether the post looks professional, or whether the mathematics is right.
proposals.rationale: MODE 4 typographic and markup habit. The slice splits sharply: R03 contains no mathematical markup at all and writes '5^10 = 9,765,625' and '3.68 x 10^-6'; R39 writes 'a*x^{1/2}' and '1/2*a*x^{-1/2}' with asterisk products; R10 writes prime factorisations with asterisks and pastes raw tool output. Against these, R19 opens by defining a macro, R34 uses align-star blocks with coloured emphasis throughout, R38 uses tagged equations and full determinant arrays, and R22 closes a proof with a typographic end marker. Markup habit is a rendering property that a text-only model reads directly, and it indexes how long the author has been writing in this format rather than whether sibling voters preferred this answer. Mixed because a practised regular may both typeset better and argue better.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's tenure and practice with the site's markup conventions

proposals.name: Hint register: withheld completion and work handed back
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH OF THE POST IS A NUDGE RATHER THAN A COMPLETED DERIVATION. Raise the score for: an explicit 'Hint' or 'HINT' opener; bare imperative pointers ('Note that', 'Complete the square', 'Use the integral expression for the Gamma function', 'Show that', 'Consider', 'Then let t = ...'); work explicitly deferred to the reader ('I leave it to you to simplify this expression', 'Now you have to figure out when it becomes periodic', a labelled 'HOMEWORK 1' exercise, 'How would you modify step 3?'); Socratic questions handed back ('Can you think of an x1 and x2 that meet these requirements?'); and stopping before the final quantity is produced. Lower the score for a self-contained derivation carried through to its stated conclusion. 0 = fully worked, nothing withheld; 5 = a partial development that stops midway; 10 = a pure hint with essentially all work deferred. Score the EXTENT of withholding only. Do NOT judge whether hinting is the appropriate, generous or pedagogically correct choice here.
proposals.rationale: MODE 4 practised-regular terseness plus MODE 2 site norms. The hint register is dense in this slice and highly stereotyped: R04 opens 'Hint: We know that ... Then we just pick out the ones of order 6', R07 opens 'Hint. Note that' and ends 'Finally let t = ...', R30 is 'Hint: Complete the square' with a bare answer, R37 is a single hint sentence, R54 is 'HINT: Work up to it in steps', R41 opens 'HINT', R42 ends by asking the reader to supply the witnesses, R26 says 'I leave it you to simplify this expression', R06 says 'Now you have to figure out when it becomes periodic'. Whether a post hints or completes is driven by the answering norms the author has internalised for homework-shaped questions, not by whether that question's voters ranked it above its siblings. Mixed because a well-judged hint can also be genuinely what a reader wants.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the format and adherence to the site's homework-answering norms

proposals.name: Second-person auditing of the asker's own attempt
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW DIRECTLY THE POST ADDRESSES THE INDIVIDUAL ASKER AND THEIR SPECIFIC WORK rather than a general future reader. Raise the score for: second-person pronouns aimed at the asker; explicit reference to the asker's own posted attempt, notation, diagram, matrices or arithmetic ('Your DFA looks good to me', 'You just made a little arithmetic mistake near the end', 'You mixed them up', 'You seem to be greatly confused', 'Your matrices A(n) are parts of the infinite matrix', 'If, as you did, w = e^{iz}', 'from your own remarks', 'As pointed out in the question'); localisation of an error to a specific line of the asker's work; and closing checks aimed at that person ('Does that make sense?'). Lower it for impersonal exposition addressed to anyone. 0 = no address to the asker at all; 5 = occasional second person but no engagement with their attempt; 10 = the whole post is a line-by-line audit of the asker's own working. Score EXTENT of asker-directed address only. Do NOT judge whether the diagnosis is helpful, courteous or correct.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2 upstream (a live back-and-forth with one person, which requires being present early) with the MODE 4 relationship-to-reader prior. R55 is entirely an audit of the asker's algebra ('You did it correctly. You just made a little arithmetic mistake near the end'); R21 opens 'You mixed them up'; R40 opens 'You seem to be greatly confused on a couple of concepts'; R58 opens 'Your DFA looks good to me. I don't know what you mean by...'; R52 diagnoses 'your method isn't counting scenarios like...'; R22 and R28 both build on the asker's own notation; R32 closes 'Does that make sense?'. The visible fingerprint is of a dialogue, which is a function of arrival timing and the asker's presence, not of the crowd's comparative judgement of sibling answers. Mixed because responsiveness to the actual attempt can also be genuine merit.
proposals.upstream_parent: a live exchange with the asker (early arrival in the thread, ongoing comment dialogue)

proposals.name: Supplementary framing presupposing an already-populated thread
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH THE TEXT PRESUPPOSES THAT OTHER ANSWERS ALREADY EXIST. Raise the score for: explicit reference to sibling answers or their authors ('This is a complimentary note to MichaelNgelo and Sherushe's answers', 'Essentially the same as TheSilverDoe's but much simplified', 'This second answer gives a shorter proof, more algebraic, which does not expand on your ideas', 'probably a variant of what Qiaochu Yuan had in mind', 'This case is already nicely considered in the answer from ErickWong', 'mesel's answer about why ... is very good', 'As shown in this post and in the accepted answer'); additive or alternative framing ('Another point of view towards', 'Also note that', 'More conceptually', 'I will provide a geometric proof', 'I still felt like a complete proof using graph theory might add something to this thread', 'As mentioned before', 'I know that you ask about non-graph approaches in particular'); and any completeness or alternative-route move. Lower the score when the post engages the raw question from scratch as though nothing had yet been said. 0 = wholly from scratch, no awareness of any other answer; 5 = a single additive connective with no named reference; 10 = the post is explicitly positioned as an addendum to identified existing answers. Score EXTENT of the presupposition only. Do NOT judge whether adding to the thread was warranted or whether the addition is valuable.
proposals.rationale: MODE 3, position in container. The fingerprint is unusually explicit here and heavily concentrated on one side of the disagreement: R14 opens 'This is a complimentary note to MichaelNgelo and Sherushe's answers', R11 opens with a parenthetical crediting TheSilverDoe, R19 opens 'This second answer gives a shorter proof', R23 says the proof 'might add something to this thread', R31 defers the first half to mesel's answer, R15 credits Qiaochu Yuan, R34 hands a case off to another answerer, R16 opens 'Another point view towards', R36 opens 'More conceptually', R57 cites the accepted answer of a linked post, R44 announces 'I will provide a geometric proof', R59 opens 'Also note that'. Arrival position determines both this phrasing and how many readers ever reach the post; it is not itself the within-question crowd preference. Mixed because a later answerer can genuinely improve on what already stands.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the answer arrival order (how many answers already stood when this was written)

proposals.name: Social-graph and standing markers: handles, self-citation, credentials
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH THE TEXT DISPLAYS THE AUTHOR'S EMBEDDEDNESS AND STANDING IN THIS COMMUNITY. Raise the score for: at-handles and other users' usernames used familiarly; reference to comments the author themself left ('the comment I gave above', 'as mfl says'); self-citation of the author's own other posts or publications ('As in my post', 'I answered a similar answer showing how to perform the LU decomposition', 'in my book, curves are always treated as parametrized curves', 'see Chapter 6 in my book'); professional or institutional self-identification ('My colleague, Chris Cooper, has written up some notes for a discrete math course we teach here at Macquarie University'); announcements of forthcoming work and solicitations of feedback in an authorial voice ('I'm going to be working on a second edition ... I welcome suggestions'); and a signed personal name at the foot of the post. 0 = anonymous prose with none of these; 5 = one such marker; 10 = several distinct standing or social-graph markers. Score EXTENT of the visible markers only. Do NOT judge whether the author is authoritative, whether the credentials are impressive, or whether name-dropping is tasteful.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2, factor (a) reputation and following, with the textual fingerprint required by (b) and (c). R48 refers twice to 'my book', announces a second edition, invites suggestions and is signed with a personal name; R58 names a colleague and the university where the author teaches; R25 self-cites a prior answer of its own; R05 says 'As in my post'; R28 refers to 'the comment I gave above'; R34 and R48 both address other users by handle; R11 and R42 name other answerers. Standing and following affect how many readers a post reaches and how they arrive at it - upstream of reception rather than identical to sibling-comparison preference - and it leaves exactly these traces in the text. Mixed because established regulars plausibly also write better answers.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's standing, tenure and following on the site

proposals.name: Edit scars, provisionality and admitted uncertainty
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW VISIBLY THE POST CARRIES MARKS OF REVISION AND PROVISIONAL STATUS. Raise the score for: literal revision labels and appended blocks that clearly postdate the original text ('edit:', 'Edit:', 'EDIT: I have three suggestions', 'P.S.', 'Note: This answer has the focus to ...', '2nd note:'); hedged or self-doubting framing of the author's own contribution ('I think I have the answer using generating functions', 'I'm not sure if that solves the problem - there might be an error elsewhere', 'I am not 100 percent sure that you weren't aware of all that already', 'no promise that they will be helpful', 'probably a variant of'); explicit self-flagging of trouble in one's own text ('and well, this is broken'); and unresolved loose ends left standing at the end. Lower the score for a single clean pass delivered flatly and declaratively. 0 = no revision marks and no hedging; 5 = one edit label or one hedge; 10 = several revision labels together with repeated explicit provisionality. Score EXTENT of the visible revision and provisionality marks only. Do NOT judge whether the hedging is warranted, whether the edits improved the post, or whether the mathematics is right.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2, factor (a) process dynamics on the receiving side, made textual per (b) and (c). Post-hoc patching is legible in the slice: R12 ends 'edit: And well, this is broken'; R32 appends 'Edit: I wouldn't worry about it too much'; R58 appends 'EDIT: I have three suggestions ... and no promise that they will be helpful'; R28 says outright 'I'm not sure if that solves the problem - there might be an error elsewhere'; R18 appends a '2nd note' conceding uncertainty about what the asker already knew; R05 opens 'I think I have the answer'; R34 opens with a scope 'Note:'. The scar records that readers reacted and the author returned - a process fact, not the crowd's comparative ranking of siblings. Mixed because revision under scrutiny may also genuinely improve the content.
proposals.upstream_parent: process dynamics after posting (readers' comments prompting patches and appendices)

proposals.name: Generic tutor-assistant scaffolding register
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW CLOSELY THE PROSE FOLLOWS A GENERIC TUTORIAL-ASSISTANT TEMPLATE. Raise the score for: an opening that restates the task and announces a method ('To solve this problem, we can use a combination of probability and combinatorial analysis'); uniform discourse scaffolding across paragraphs ('First, let's consider ...', 'Now, let's consider ...', 'To find ..., we can ...', 'Finally, to find ..., we can ...'); every stage closing with a 'Therefore, ...' restatement; a closing sentence that spells the computed result back out as a full sentence ('Therefore, the expected value of the number of times the number 3 is drawn in a sequence of 10 numbers is 2'); evenly paced hedge-free narration of routine steps at uniform grain, with no asides, no shortcuts and no idiosyncratic voice; decimal or ASCII numeric formatting; and no venue-specific idiom. Lower the score for uneven human prose that jumps, digresses, or assumes shared context. 0 = idiosyncratic voice throughout; 5 = template-like in places; 10 = the template runs end to end. Score EXTENT of the visible register only. Do NOT judge whether the reasoning inside is correct, and do NOT try to decide who or what wrote the post - score the register as it appears.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2, factor (a) editing or assistance, with the required visible fingerprint. R03 runs the template end to end - it restates the task, marches through 'First, let's consider ... Now, let's consider ... To find ... Finally', writes numbers as '5^10 = 9,765,625' and '3.68 x 10^-6', and closes by restating the result as a sentence; R39 shows the flatter variant, announcing 'Given the form of the function, you know', then 'Therefore', 'Then', 'Therefore', with asterisk-product ASCII throughout; R35 shows a mild case with its announced 'engineering explanation' framing. The register indexes how and when a post was composed, which is orthogonal to sibling-comparison preference, so it is tagged not-mixed: uniform scaffolding is a stylistic signature, not itself a reason a question's voters preferred one answer over its siblings.
proposals.upstream_parent: machine-assisted composition and post recency (which era of the corpus the post comes from)

proposals.name: Content sourced elsewhere: links, citations, pasted tool output
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH OF THE POST'S SUBSTANCE IS DEFERRED TO OR TRANSPLANTED FROM SOMETHING OUTSIDE THE POST. Raise the score for: bare or near-bare URLs standing in for the explanation ('http colon slash slash en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_projective_plane - Look at the first two pictures on the right'); pointers to other questions or threads on the site ('See for example How many subgroups of order n does D_n have?'); a bibliographic citation carrying the answer (a journal reference given as the whole reply, or a pasted review record with an identifier, reviewer name and full abstract); pasted output or transcripts of an external computational tool (session lines such as 'In[383]:= ... Out[383]=', or appeals to what 'Mathematica uses' or what 'Wolfram Alpha says'); and referrals to offline or unlocated material ('My colleague ... has written up some notes ... I don't have the URL handy, but you might find the notes if you do a little sniffing about'). 0 = wholly self-contained prose and derivation; 5 = self-contained argument with one supporting pointer; 10 = the post is essentially a pointer, a citation or a paste. Score EXTENT of external sourcing only. Do NOT judge whether the reference is apt, authoritative, sufficient or correctly attributed.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2, factor (a) resources and assistance available to the producer, expressed as a visible trace. R53 is a bare Wikipedia URL plus an instruction to look at the pictures; R04 is a hint plus a link to another question on the site; R45 is one sentence plus a 1961 Monthly citation; R41 pastes an entire review record with identifier, reviewer, journal and abstract; R10 pastes raw computer-algebra session lines with input and output prompt numbers; R58 refers the reader to a colleague's unlocated notes; R08 answers by reporting what a computer-algebra system does; R28 appeals to what an online engine reports for a special case. Access to literature and tools varies with seniority and setting, so the trace is upstream of reception rather than being sibling-comparison preference itself. Mixed because a well-chosen reference or a tool-checked step can also be genuine merit.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's access to literature and tooling, and the habit of curating rather than composing

proposals.name: Diagnostic engagement with asker's own work
proposals.instruction: Score how directly the answer engages with the SPECIFIC work, notation, or claims the asker already produced in their post, as opposed to giving a generic solution addressed to nobody in particular. A 10: the answer quotes or paraphrases the asker's own steps/equations and pinpoints exactly where they are right or wrong (e.g. 'you made a mistake near the end', 'your DFA looks good'). A 0: the answer could be pasted verbatim onto any similarly-themed question with no reference to what the asker specifically wrote.
proposals.rationale: R33 and R46 both walk through the asker's own derivation line-by-line to locate the error/confusion; R36 and R40 open by directly evaluating the asker's stated approach ('Nope!', addressing 'you' and their equations). These personalized-tutoring answers cluster in dense_high_card_low, suggesting the dense model rewards this responsiveness in a way a criteria scorecard, grading generic content quality, does not.

proposals.name: Conversational personal voice and asides
proposals.instruction: Score the presence of an informal, personal authorial voice: rhetorical questions to the reader, humor, opinions, or asides not strictly required by the math. 10 = answer reads like a person talking to another person, with visible personality/opinion; 0 = purely impersonal, formal exposition with no first/second-person commentary beyond bare necessity.
proposals.rationale: R49 ends with 'Does that make sense?' plus an opinionated aside that stem-leaf plots are 'kind of silly'; R11 hedges with 'no promise that they will be helpful'. Both are dense_high_card_low, suggesting this informal voice is something the dense model picks up on that a criterion-bank judge scoring formal content quality would not reward.

proposals.name: Self-flagged uncertainty or error in own reasoning
proposals.instruction: Score how explicitly the answer flags its own uncertainty, incompleteness, or a mistake in its own working. 10 = answer explicitly says something like 'I'm not sure this is right' or 'this is broken' or admits a step might fail; 0 = the answer states everything with unqualified confidence, without any self-doubt language.
proposals.rationale: R24 ends with 'edit: And well, this is broken', and R22 admits 'I'm not sure if that solves the problem - there might be an error elsewhere'. Both are dense_high_card_low despite the visible self-doubt, which a scorecard grading confidence/correctness would likely penalize.

proposals.name: Full derivation to closure vs. bare pointer/hint
proposals.instruction: Score where the answer sits between a bare pointer and a fully closed derivation. 10 = the answer works the problem through to an explicit final result with no steps left for the reader to fill in; 0 = the answer only names a technique or gives a one-line hint ('use X') and stops, leaving the actual work undone.
proposals.rationale: R02 ('Hint: Use the integral expression for the Gamma function...') and R07 ('Hint. Note that...') are terse pointers that are dense_high_card_low, while R21 and R60 carry a generating-function or number-theoretic argument all the way to a stated conclusion and are dense_low_card_high - suggesting the scorecard rewards closure that the dense model does not require.

proposals.name: Justification outsourced to an unreproduced citation
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the answer's core justification depends on an external reference (a link, a named colleague's notes, a quoted review, a cited paper) that is NOT reproduced or explained within the answer itself. 10 = the decisive argument is 'see this link/paper/person's notes' with no independent derivation given; 0 = every claim is derived or explained within the text itself.
proposals.rationale: R11 says 'My colleague...has written up some notes...I don't have the URL handy' and R57 answers with only 'It is enough to use only horizontal and vertical lines' plus a bare journal citation. Both are dense_high_card_low, suggesting outsourced justification is something the dense model tolerates or rewards that a scorecard tied to self-contained rigor would not.

proposals.name: Concrete worked numeric/computational instantiation
proposals.instruction: Score the presence of concrete worked numbers or computed intermediate values (plugging in actual integers, showing a step-by-step numeric computation or software output) as opposed to purely abstract symbolic argument. 10 = answer shows multiple explicit worked numeric examples or computed outputs; 0 = the answer stays entirely at the level of general symbols/variables with no concrete instantiation.
proposals.rationale: R01 shows explicit computed outputs for pi, e, and e^10, and R43 walks a specific 3x3 numeric matrix through Gaussian elimination step by step. Both are dense_high_card_low despite very different mathematical soundness, suggesting concrete numeric texture itself (not correctness) is what the dense model is picking up on.

proposals.name: Confident technical surface despite unclear validity
proposals.instruction: Score the INTERACTION of (a) heavy technical apparatus - dense notation, symbolic manipulation, or computed outputs - together with (b) an assertive, unhedged presentation, evaluated independently of whether the underlying mathematics is actually sound. 10 = answer presents elaborate notation/computation in a fully confident, declarative register even where a careful reader would find the argument questionable or incomplete; 0 = answer is notation-light and/or visibly tentative throughout.
proposals.rationale: R01 presents an elaborate 'canonical real factorization' construction with confident declarative prose ('Perfect, we capture all the reals like we desired') despite the underlying claim being mathematically dubious; R23 presents a confident multi-paragraph combinatorial derivation that is internally inconsistent. Both are dense_high_card_low with very low card_pct, suggesting the scorecard penalizes the shaky substance while the dense model may be responding to the confident technical surface.

proposals.name: Explicit structural signposting of steps/parts
proposals.instruction: Score the use of explicit structural markers - numbered steps ('Step 1', 'Step 2'), labeled sections, or part headers ('First question:', 'Second question:') - that make the answer's organization visible on the page. 10 = answer is visibly segmented with numbered/labeled steps or parts; 0 = answer is one undifferentiated block of prose/math with no visible structural markers.
proposals.rationale: R10 is organized into 'Step 1' through 'Step 4' and R25 is explicitly split into 'First question:' and 'Second question:' sections. Both are dense_low_card_high, suggesting the scorecard rewards visible organizational scaffolding that the dense model does not specifically credit.

proposals.name: Generalization beyond the literal question asked
proposals.instruction: Score whether the answer extends past the literal question to state a broader theorem, generalize the method to a wider class of cases, or pose a related extended problem. 10 = answer explicitly generalizes (e.g. 'the same technique works for...', 'more generally, X^n/Y^(n-1) for all n') or offers a related follow-up problem; 0 = answer addresses only the exact narrow instance asked and nothing more.
proposals.rationale: R03 extends its cube-root-of-unity trick to a second, more complicated polynomial unprompted, and R20 notes the general fact 'D^n/S^(n-1) is homeomorphic to S^n for all n' beyond the specific disk/sphere case asked. Both are dense_low_card_high, suggesting this generalizing move is rewarded by the scorecard in a way the dense model undervalues.

proposals.name: Intuition-first pedagogical exposition for general audience
proposals.instruction: Score how much the answer builds motivating intuition (analogies, 'why' framing, conceptual scaffolding) accessible beyond the narrow technical question, rather than launching straight into formal manipulation. 10 = answer opens with or foregrounds an intuitive/motivating framing (analogy, real-world comparison) before or alongside the formalism; 0 = answer is purely formal/technical from the first line with zero motivating exposition.
proposals.rationale: R08 builds an extended letter/questions analogy to motivate Shannon entropy before touching the formula, and R31 gives an 'engineering explanation' with a concrete sampling-grid analogy. Both are dense_low_card_high, suggesting this pedagogical framing is rewarded by the scorecard in a way the dense model does not specifically pick up on.

proposals.name: Situates itself relative to other answers on thread
proposals.instruction: Score whether the answer explicitly positions itself with respect to other answers already visible in context (building on, complementing, offering a shorter/alternate proof to, or citing another named answerer), as opposed to standing as an isolated response. 10 = answer explicitly references and relates itself to another specific answer/answerer; 0 = answer makes no reference to any other answer and reads as a freestanding, isolated response.
proposals.rationale: R37 opens 'This second answer gives a shorter proof, more algebraic, which does not expand on your ideas' and R58 calls itself 'a complimentary note to MichaelNgelo and Sherushe's answers'. Both are dense_low_card_high, suggesting this thread-awareness is a scorecard-rewarded property the dense model is not tracking.

proposals.name: Coverage of every part of a multi-part question
proposals.instruction: If the question, as excerpted, contains multiple distinct sub-questions or requests (e.g. 'First... Second...', multiple named unknowns, or several explicit asks), score how completely the answer addresses ALL of them versus only a subset. 10 = every distinct part/sub-question visible in the prompt is explicitly taken up and resolved in the answer; 0 = the answer addresses only one part (or a tangential aspect) and is silent on the other explicit parts. If the question has only a single part, score based on whether the answer treats that single ask as fully resolved (10) or leaves an unaddressed remainder implied by the question's phrasing (0).
proposals.rationale: R25 is explicitly organized to answer 'First question:' and 'Second question:' from the underlying prompt in full, and R59 works through numbered parts '1.' and '2.' of the asker's problem to completion. Both are dense_low_card_high, suggesting the scorecard rewards exhaustive coverage of everything asked in a way the dense model does not specifically track.

proposals.name: Terse notation-heavy fragment with minimal prose
proposals.instruction: Score how much the answer consists of dense mathematical notation/equations presented with minimal connecting prose or explanation of what the notation means or why each step follows - i.e., an expert-only fragment that assumes the reader can fill in all the reasoning themselves. 10 = the answer is almost entirely symbols/equations with at most one or two short unexplained sentences; 0 = every symbolic step is accompanied by explanatory prose making the reasoning legible to a non-expert reader.
proposals.rationale: R04 answers 'Note that e_i is an orthonormal vector field wrt ds^2. Hence we let the dual frame...' with essentially no elaboration of why, and R14 states a full non-unital ring classification in three dense lines with minimal connective explanation. Both are dense_low_card_high, suggesting the scorecard tolerates or rewards this expert-shorthand terseness in a way distinct from the discursive hint-style terseness the dense model favors (contrast R02's 'Hint: Use...' phrasing).

proposals.name: Blunt correction paired with full independent justification
proposals.instruction: Score the INTERACTION of two features: (a) the answer opens by bluntly stating that the asker's premise/claim is wrong (e.g. 'This is wrong', 'Nope!', 'not satisfied'), AND (b) the answer then supplies a complete, independently verifiable justification for that correction (a constructed counterexample, explicit computation, or full argument) rather than resting on the blunt assertion alone. 10 = both a direct blunt correction AND a fully worked, self-contained justification are present; 0 = neither a direct blunt correction nor supporting justification is present (e.g. the answer is hedging or purely affirmative with no corrective claim).
proposals.rationale: R09 opens 'This is wrong' and then constructs a full explicit counterexample sequence with the required properties proven, and R45 states directly that 'the condition of your statement is not satisfied' and immediately proves it. Both are dense_low_card_high. This contrasts with R36, which also opens with a blunt 'Nope!' correction but follows with only a brief, informal clarification rather than a fully independent derivation, and is dense_high_card_low - suggesting it is the PAIRING of bluntness with full justification, not bluntness alone, that the scorecard rewards.

proposals.name: Explicit statement of conditions under which result holds
proposals.instruction: Score whether the answer explicitly identifies and states the specific conditions, assumptions, or boundary cases under which its claimed result is valid, as opposed to asserting a conclusion unconditionally or leaving the scope of validity implicit. 10 = answer explicitly enumerates the conditions/cases needed (e.g. 'if f'(x0) > -1 then...', case-by-case conditions on parity/divisibility); 0 = answer states its conclusion as an unqualified blanket claim with no stated conditions or case distinctions.
proposals.rationale: R42 explicitly conditions its no-shock conclusion on 'If f'(x0) > -1' and R38 works through an elaborate case analysis on the parity of k and whether q is a perfect square before stating when a solution m exists. Both are dense_low_card_high, suggesting the scorecard rewards this precise scoping of validity in a way the dense model does not specifically track.

proposals.name: Hint-only pointer style vs full derivation
proposals.instruction: 0-10: how much this answer is written as a terse HINT or pointer (e.g., opens with 'Hint:'/'HINT', gives a starting idea, formula, or reference and stops) rather than a complete worked derivation to a final result. 0 = fully worked, self-contained derivation with no hint framing; 10 = answer is essentially just a hint/pointer with little to no completed derivation. Score only how hint-like/incomplete the presentation is -- do NOT judge whether the hint is a good hint or whether the underlying idea is correct.
proposals.rationale: R10 ('Hint. Note that...'), R13 ('Hint: Use the integral expression...'), R19 ('HINT: Work up to it in steps'), R25 ('Hint: Complete the square... Answer: 13'), R51 ('HINT Your polynomial...'), R60 ('Hint: We know that...') all stop at a pointer rather than a worked solution; this template phrase is plausibly predictive of the disagreement slice independent of whether voters actually preferred the item.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Casual interjection/ellipsis punctuation density
proposals.instruction: 0-10: how much the answer uses informal interjection punctuation -- run-on ellipses ('..', '...'), exclamation marks, or parenthetical asides that break the mathematical flow. 0 = no such informal punctuation, uniformly formal prose; 10 = pervasive informal punctuation throughout. Do not judge whether the informality is charming or off-putting, only score its extent.
proposals.rationale: R03 ('though rather dangerous! .. see paragraph below', '.. that there different'), R23 ('Edit: I wouldn't worry about it too much... kind of silly'), and R47 ('edit: And well, this is broken.') all carry this orthographic quirk; it is a typography tell rather than a within-question preference signal.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Narrated step-by-step tutorial scaffolding phrases
proposals.instruction: 0-10: how much the answer uses explicit narrating/scaffolding transition phrases that talk the reader through the process in tutorial voice ('Let's...', 'Now let's...', 'First, ... Now, ... Finally, ...'). 0 = no such narrating transitions; 10 = the answer is structured almost entirely around this narrated-walkthrough voice. Score only the presence/frequency of this phrasing, not whether the walkthrough is pedagogically effective.
proposals.rationale: R04 ('First, let's consider...', 'Now, let's consider...', 'Finally, to find...') and R17 ('Now let's unwrap it piece by piece', 'let's have a closer look at entropy') both lean heavily on this scaffolding register, a stylistic habit distinct from within-question quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Verbatim computational-tool output or citation
proposals.instruction: 0-10: how much the answer contains verbatim output from, or explicit naming of, an external computational/symbolic tool (e.g. 'Wolfram Alpha says...', 'Mathematica uses...', or REPL-style transcript syntax like 'In[383]:=' / 'Out[383]='). 0 = no tool mention or tool-output formatting; 10 = extensive tool-output transcript is a major part of the answer. Score only the presence of this tool-citation fingerprint, not whether the tool's result is correct or well-used.
proposals.rationale: R01 ('Wolfram Alpha says when n=2 the numerator is...'), R49 ('Mathematica uses the range...'), and R50 (pastes literal 'In[383]:=' / 'Out[383]=' transcripts) all carry this fingerprint of an upstream authoring practice that could bias a text-only model regardless of within-question quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice of using/citing external symbolic-computation tools when composing an answer

proposals.name: Post-hoc edit/update annotation marker
proposals.instruction: 0-10: how much the answer contains an explicit marker indicating it was revised or appended after initial posting (e.g. 'Edit:', 'EDIT:', 'Update:', 'P.S.'). 0 = no such marker; 10 = the answer is structured around one or more clearly labeled edit/update/P.S. sections. Score only the presence of the marker, not what the edit says or whether it improves the answer.
proposals.rationale: R23 ('Edit: I wouldn't worry about it too much...'), R47 ('edit: And well, this is broken.'), R58 ('EDIT: I have three suggestions...'), and R59 ('P.S. $e_n=...$') all carry an explicit revision marker, a submission-process trace rather than a direct quality signal.
proposals.upstream_parent: editing/revision process occurring after the answer's initial submission

proposals.name: Answerer's disclosed professional identity/authority
proposals.instruction: 0-10: how much the answer discloses the author's real-world professional identity, institutional affiliation, or authored publications (e.g. signing a real full name, saying 'in my book', naming a university where they teach, naming a named colleague's course notes). 0 = fully anonymous, no such disclosure; 10 = explicit name/affiliation/authored-work disclosure is prominent. Score only the presence of such disclosure, not whether the disclosed credentials are impressive.
proposals.rationale: R46 signs 'Jack Lee' and references 'in my book' / 'my Riemannian Manifolds book', and R58 discloses 'My colleague, Chris Cooper, has written up some notes for a discrete math course we teach here at Macquarie University' -- both disclose upstream authority that could bias a text model independent of this item's within-question standing.
proposals.upstream_parent: answerer's real-world reputation, seniority, or professional standing

proposals.name: Direct engagement quoting asker's specific attempted steps
proposals.instruction: 0-10: how much the answer directly quotes, reproduces, or precisely points to specific steps/expressions the asker themselves wrote, as opposed to restating or solving the bare question from scratch without reference to the asker's own work. 0 = answer engages only the abstract question, no reference to asker's specific attempt; 10 = answer is built around walking through the asker's own posted steps and pinpointing them. Score only how much the text engages the asker's specific prior work, not whether that engagement is correct or well-judged.
proposals.rationale: R15 ('You did it correctly. You just made a little arithmetic mistake near the end. You got to here... correctly but the line beneath that is not correct'), R42 ('If, as you did, $w=e^{iz}$, then your equation becomes...'), R29 ('You seem to be greatly confused on a couple of concepts'), and R30 ('as mfl says, you can infer the existence...') all show this engagement mode, a process trace distinct from the answer's own merit.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing / thread engagement -- the answerer read and responded to the asker's own posted attempt rather than answering cold

proposals.name: Explicit self-doubt or uncertainty hedge about own answer
proposals.instruction: 0-10: how much the answer explicitly voices uncertainty or self-doubt about its own correctness or completeness (e.g. 'I'm not sure if that solves the problem', 'I think I have the answer', 'I am not 100% sure'). 0 = no such hedge, confidently declarative throughout; 10 = the answer repeatedly flags its own uncertainty. Score only the presence of this hedging language, not whether the underlying math is actually right or wrong.
proposals.rationale: R01 ('I'm not sure if that solves the problem - there might be an error elsewhere'), R56 ('I think I have the answer using generating functions'), and R05 ('I am not 100% sure that you weren't aware of all that already') all carry this hedging fingerprint, an upstream confidence trace rather than a direct correctness signal.
proposals.upstream_parent: answerer's confidence level / relative expertise in this specific subfield

proposals.name: Presupposes or names sibling answers on this question
proposals.instruction: 0-10: how much the answer's language presupposes that other answers to the SAME question already exist, or explicitly references them (e.g. naming another answerer by username, saying 'this second answer', 'a complementary note to X and Y's answers', 'essentially the same as X's but simplified', referring back to 'this post' as already having covered related ground). 0 = the answer reads as if engaging the raw question from scratch with no awareness of other answers; 10 = the answer is explicitly framed as a response to, or addition alongside, specific other answers. Score only this presupposition/reference, not whether the comparison it draws is accurate or fair.
proposals.rationale: R26 ('Essentially the same as TheSilverDoe's but much simplified'), R31 ('This is a complimentary note to MichaelNgelo and Sherushe's answers'), R48 ('mesel's answer about why 2sin(10 degrees) satisfies x^3-3x+1=0 is very good'), and R53 ('This second answer gives a shorter proof, more algebraic') all show explicit awareness of co-existing answers, a container-position trace rather than a within-question quality signal.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the answer-arrival order -- composed after seeing other answers already posted in the thread

proposals.name: Question framed as open 'intuition'/conceptual request
proposals.instruction: 0-10: how much the QUESTION this answer is attached to is framed as an open-ended request for intuition or conceptual understanding (e.g. titled or phrased 'Intuitive explanation of X', 'What is the intuition behind X') rather than as a closed, routine computational task with a single numeric or symbolic target. 0 = question is a narrow, closed computational request; 10 = question is explicitly and broadly framed as an intuition/conceptual request. Score only the question's framing, not the quality of the answer that follows.
proposals.rationale: R17 and R31 both answer the question 'Intuitive explanation of entropy', and R57 answers 'What is the intuition behind simple Lie groups?' -- all three draw long, discursive, essay-style answers, showing the question's own framing is plausibly predictive of item length/register independent of within-question crowd preference.
proposals.upstream_parent: the kind of question this answer is attached to -- a conceptual, crowd-drawing question versus a routine homework computation

proposals.name: Guided next-step usefulness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the answer identifies and executes the decisive next operation while leaving only routine work; score 0 when it provides no actionable mathematical step.
proposals.rationale: Hints such as R10, R36, R42, and R47 expose the key move efficiently, a feature raw text can value even when a checklist rewards only completed derivations.

proposals.name: Complete task resolution
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the answer reaches the requested conclusion and supports it sufficiently; score 0 when it merely restates the problem, gives background, or stops before resolution.
proposals.rationale: R02, R09, and R22 carry arguments through to a conclusion, whereas R40, R42, and R46 stop at partial guidance; this separates useful completeness from superficial detail.

proposals.name: Exact error repair
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the answer pinpoints a specific mistake, supplies the corrected expression or argument, and explains the correction; score 0 when criticism is vague or absent.
proposals.rationale: R23 and R51 give sharply localized corrections, while R29 and R55 illustrate how merely identifying or overlooking a flaw can mislead despite mathematical-looking prose.

proposals.name: Verification against the setup
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the answer checks its conclusion against the original equations, definitions, boundary conditions, or a construction; score 0 when no meaningful check is made.
proposals.rationale: R02 and R22 explicitly verify the constructed objects, while R51 and R53 leave verification to the reader; this may explain why short, testable answers are distinguished from elaborate unchecked ones.

proposals.name: Assumption and edge-case control
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when all relevant domains, exceptional cases, branch choices, and limiting conditions are stated and handled; score 0 when such conditions are silently ignored.
proposals.rationale: R06, R16, R31, and R59 show how convergence and inverse-function conventions matter, while R23 exposes a missed counting case.

proposals.name: Concept-to-example bridge
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an abstract idea is connected to a concrete example or mental model and then tied back to the formal claim; score 0 when the answer remains abstract or uses an analogy without mathematical linkage.
proposals.rationale: R01, R11, and R15 attempt intuitive bridges for entropy, while R37 uses an informal infinity analogy; the quality of the bridge can matter independently of technical sophistication.

proposals.name: Explicit justification continuity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when every nontrivial transition is connected by a stated reason, theorem, or calculation; score 0 when major claims appear as unexplained assertions.
proposals.rationale: R03 and R42 contain substantial inferential gaps, whereas R09 and R18 make many intermediate dependencies explicit; this captures explanatory continuity rather than length alone.

proposals.name: Notation and convention stability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when symbols, operation order, inverse-function conventions, and parameter meanings are clearly fixed and used consistently; score 0 when notation is ambiguous, contradictory, or convention-sensitive without clarification.
proposals.rationale: R17 and R45 depend on composition order, while R31, R43, and R59 depend on inverse-function or parametrization conventions.

proposals.name: Question-specific relevance
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when essentially every substantial sentence addresses the exact question asked; score 0 when the answer is mostly generic background, unrelated literature, or ornamental discussion.
proposals.rationale: R30 and R44 wander into broad contextual material, while R10 and R23 stay tightly focused on the local question; this distinction is visible from text alone.

proposals.name: Proportionate explanatory detail
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the amount and granularity of explanation fit the problem and reader's apparent need; score 0 when the answer is severely too terse or burdensomely overdeveloped for its task.
proposals.rationale: R01 and R15 are extensive treatments of intuition, whereas R42 and R52 are extremely compressed; R10 and R51 illustrate concise responses calibrated to a specific obstruction.

proposals.name: Method fidelity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the answer follows the requested method or explicitly explains a justified change of method; score 0 when it ignores a stated methodological constraint without acknowledgment.
