Experienced users are more willing to be terse and give only the key insight, and their hints may genuinely be more valuable. But the format itself is a practice/habit signal that confounds with content quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice and confidence in the format

proposals.name: Structured proof scaffolding
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the answer uses explicit structural scaffolding: numbered or bolded step labels (e.g. 'Step 1', 'Step 2'), section headers, nested case-analysis markers with indentation, or algorithmic step-by-step formatting with intermediate updates. Do not judge whether the structure aids comprehension.
proposals.rationale: R16 uses 'Step 1' through 'Step 4' in bold with congruence arguments; R35 uses heavily structured case analysis with coloured highlights and constraint headers; R50 presents step-by-step algorithm updates with labelled matrices; R58 uses numbered sections '1.' and '2.' The scorecard rewards this visible organisation; the dense model may discount it because scaffolding does not necessarily make the mathematics more correct or insightful. Authors with teaching experience both write more structured answers and may provide clearer explanations, making this factor mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's teaching practice and formatting habits

proposals.name: Raw answer length
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 based on the total word and token count of the answer text including all mathematics. 0 = extremely short (under 20 words), 5 = moderate (approximately 100-200 words), 10 = very long (over 500 words). Do not judge whether the length is appropriate or excessive.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high items like R03 (three lines including a self-correction), R17 (two sentences), R23 (three sentences correcting a misconception), R28 (one sentence) are among the shortest. Dense-low items like R02, R09, R25, R55, R58 are among the longest. Length is a surface feature that both models likely use as a proxy -- longer answers trigger more scorecard criteria while shorter ones may read as confident and direct to the dense model -- but raw length does not directly reflect voter preference within a single question.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Conversational register and rhetorical engagement
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the answer uses conversational, tutorial-style register: rhetorical questions directed at the reader ('Does that make sense?', 'Can you think of...?'), informal connectives, exclamation marks, interactive prompts ('I leave it to you'), or meta-commentary about the explanation process. Do not judge whether the conversational tone is helpful or appropriate.
proposals.rationale: R09 assigns 'HOMEWORK 1' and walks through entropy with extensive hand-holding; R19 uses informal phrasing ('wrap your mind around this', 'not any two infinite sets have the same cardinality'); R29 ends 'I leave it you to simplify this expression'; R52 asks 'Does that make sense?' and editorialises ('kind of silly'). This register signals an author writing for a broad audience of future searchers. Such answers may attract upvotes from readers who appreciate accessibility, independent of mathematical depth, making the parent factor mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's relationship to the reader and intended audience

proposals.name: Display mathematics proportion
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the proportion of mathematical content presented in display mode (centred equations, $$...$$, \begin{align}, \begin{matrix}, etc.) relative to inline mathematics. 0 = almost entirely inline or no math, 10 = almost entirely in display environments. Do not judge whether the formatting choice is appropriate.
proposals.rationale: Dense-low/card-high items like R02 (multiple display equations and a matrix), R25 (large determinant displays), R41 (long chained align environment), R57 (multi-line align blocks) make heavy use of display math environments. Dense-high/card-low items like R01, R03, R17, R22, R23, R28 use minimal or entirely inline mathematics. Display math is a formatting convention of experienced users, but the choice between display and inline is a typographic habit, not a quality signal.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's typographic and markup habits

proposals.name: Direct engagement with asker's specific work
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the answer directly engages with the asker's specific attempt, working, or stated confusion: quoting the asker's formulation, using phrases like 'You did it correctly', 'As you did', 'Your method', 'You seem to be confused about', or addressing the asker by name. Do not judge whether such engagement is helpful.
proposals.rationale: R01 directly addresses the asker's method ('If you are enumerating everyone's birthday in the denominator...'); R24 says 'You did it correctly. You just made a little arithmetic mistake near the end'; R31 engages directly ('You need to choose x_1 and x_2 as a function of a'); R34 opens 'You seem to be greatly confused on a couple of concepts.' This style signals writing for the immediate asker rather than a general audience. Such answers may be more useful to the asker but less reusable for future searchers, splitting voter preference unpredictably.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's relationship to the asker versus future readers

proposals.name: Self-correction and uncertainty markers
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the answer contains explicit markers of self-correction, hedging, or admitted uncertainty: edit notes ('edit:', 'EDIT:'), phrases like 'I'm not sure', 'there might be an error', 'no promise', or visible backtracking within the answer. Do not judge whether the uncertainty or correction is warranted.
proposals.rationale: R03 includes 'edit: And well, this is broken' after presenting a flawed derivation; R57 says 'I'm not sure if that solves the problem - there might be an error elsewhere' and notes a discrepancy with Wolfram Alpha; R42 says 'no promise that they will be helpful' when offering suggestions. These markers are artifacts of the answer's production history and the author's real-time reasoning, not properties of the final mathematical content. They reflect editing dynamics that may bias models independently of voter preference.
proposals.upstream_parent: editing process and submission dynamics

proposals.name: Advanced mathematical machinery density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the answer employs advanced or specialised mathematical machinery, terminology, and notation that goes beyond standard undergraduate curriculum: Lie algebras, spectral theorems, Möbius inversion, Dynkin diagrams, Riemannian geometry, commutator subgroups, Artin maps, Stirling's formula, etc. Count distinct advanced terms and concepts; do not judge whether the advanced machinery is necessary or appropriate.
proposals.rationale: Dense-low/card-high items use heavy specialised machinery: R02 (Riemann surfaces, branch cuts, holomorphic logarithms), R21 (Lie group actions, stabiliser subgroups, immersions, embeddings), R26 (Killing form, Whitehead's Lemmas, Dynkin diagrams, Cartan-Killing classification), R58 (Möbius inversion formula, indicator functions). Dense-high/card-low items like R01, R15, R17, R22, R40 use elementary counting, basic algebra, or arithmetic. The kind of question independently affects voting: advanced topics attract fewer but more appreciative voters, and questions drawing expert crowds have different within-question preference distributions.
proposals.upstream_parent: question type and mathematical subfield

proposals.name: Misconception-targeted diagnosis
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer identifies a specific conceptual misunderstanding evidenced in the question text and directly addresses it; score 0 if the answer proceeds mechanically without engaging what the asker is confused about. Intermediate scores for partial engagement.
proposals.rationale: R07 diagnoses confusion between spanning sets and spans, R60 corrects the misconception that loops (not homotopy classes) form the group — both rated dense_high. R01 and R45 give correct but generic content without diagnosing any asker confusion, rated dense_low.

proposals.name: Progressive hint scaffolding
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer gives staged, calibrated guidance — enough to move the student forward but leaving genuine thinking, often structured as numbered hints or rhetorical questions; score 0 if it dumps a complete solution or gives only a bare final answer with no guidance.
proposals.rationale: R02, R03, R37 all leave the final step to the student while guiding the approach — dense_high. R22 and R28 give only the answer with no scaffolding, yet score card_high.

proposals.name: Student error localization
proposals.instruction: When the question includes student work, score 10 if the answer pinpoints the exact line, term, or step where the error occurs and explains why it is wrong; score 0 if no student work is present or if the answer ignores the shown work entirely.
proposals.rationale: R47 quotes the exact correct line and the exact wrong line from the student's work; R17 identifies the specific missing factor and the uncounted scenario. Both are dense_high. R56 and R22 correct without engaging any work, rated dense_low.

proposals.name: Direct-address conversational warmth
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer speaks directly to the asker with a warm, human voice ('You seem confused…', 'Does that make sense?', 'Hopefully this shows…'); score 0 if the tone is impersonal, treating the answer as a disembodied proof dump.
proposals.rationale: R44 asks 'Does that make sense?' and adds editorial flair; R60 opens with a collegial 'Nope!' Both are dense_high. R33 and R29 read as formal proof fragments with no human address, rated dense_low.

proposals.name: Correct-work validation before correction
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer first affirms what the student did correctly before pointing out errors; score 0 if it jumps straight to corrections or if no student work is discussed.
proposals.rationale: R47 says 'You did it correctly… You just made a little arithmetic mistake'; R59 says 'Your DFA looks good to me.' Both dense_high. Dense_low items like R46 and R30 lead with 'This is wrong' or corrections without validation.

proposals.name: Intellectual humility and self-critical transparency
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer openly acknowledges its own limitations, possible errors, or uncertainty ('I'm not sure if that solves the problem', 'this is broken', 'there might be an error elsewhere'); score 0 if it presents itself as definitive with no caveats.
proposals.rationale: R19 says 'this is broken' after giving the trick; R50 admits 'I'm not sure if that solves the problem.' Both dense_high. Dense_low items like R34 and R24 present as polished, definitive proofs.

proposals.name: Concrete computation carried to completion
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer includes at least one fully worked numerical or algebraic computation from start to finish so the student can verify each step; score 0 if only final results or abstract setups are given with no worked detail.
proposals.rationale: R58 walks through every row operation with explicit arithmetic; R39 computes each digit step by step. Both dense_high. R28 and R29 give results with virtually no computation, rated dense_low.

proposals.name: Bridging analogy or simpler parallel example
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer introduces a simpler analogous problem, a known special case, or a relatable analogy that builds intuition before tackling the original question; score 0 if the answer works only with the problem as stated.
proposals.rationale: R15 uses a simpler series to illustrate the phenomenon; R18 compares N and Z via a list-making analogy. Both dense_high. R12 and R10 work directly in full generality with no bridge, rated dense_low.

proposals.name: Formalism proportionate to question level
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the level of formal notation, jargon, and machinery is well-matched to the apparent level of the question (elementary questions get elementary notation); score 0 if the answer deploys heavy formalism or advanced machinery on a question that could be answered more simply.
proposals.rationale: R14 and R08 use minimal notation for elementary questions — dense_high. R34 uses Lie group actions and equivariant maps for a question that could be more elementary; R10 uses infinite matrices where finite would suffice. Both dense_low.

proposals.name: Topical focus and answer-to-question alignment
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if every part of the answer directly serves the specific question asked; score 0 if substantial portions are tangential, generic, or address a different question than the one posed.
proposals.rationale: R25 and R36 give compact, tightly focused responses — dense_high. R45 is a general essay on the importance of simple objects; R48 drifts into textbook-author commentary. Both dense_low despite high card scores.

proposals.name: Insight-to-length efficiency
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer is concise yet each sentence carries explanatory weight — short because it is efficient, not because it is incomplete; score 0 if the answer is either bloated with redundant detail or terse to the point of being unhelpful.
proposals.rationale: R17 and R52 are short but every clause adds value — dense_high. R22 is terse and unhelpful; R40 is long and rambling. Both dense_low despite high card_pct.

proposals.name: Visual or geometric reasoning reference
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer references pictures, diagrams, geometric constructions, or invites the reader to visualize; score 0 if the answer is purely symbolic/algebraic with no spatial component.
proposals.rationale: R20 directs the reader to Wikipedia images and says 'Imagine that you cut…'; R35 provides a purely geometric proof. R20 is dense_high. Dense_low items are almost entirely symbolic (R10, R24, R27).

proposals.name: Notational convention transparency
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer explicitly discusses a choice of notation, branch, or convention and explains its consequences; score 0 if it silently assumes a convention without comment.
proposals.rationale: R52 explains Mathematica's arccot convention and offers a workaround — dense_high. R56 silently corrects a convention error with no explanation — dense_low.

proposals.name: Structured multi-step organization
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if a multi-step argument is organized into clearly labeled cases, stages, or numbered steps that a reader can follow incrementally; score 0 if the argument is a single undifferentiated block.
proposals.rationale: R05 systematically narrows cases with clearly labeled parameter ranges; R37 gives numbered steps. Both dense_high. R24 is a wall of algebra with no structural landmarks; R40 rambles without clear structure. Both dense_low.

proposals.name: Standalone self-sufficiency
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer is fully understandable on its own without needing to follow external links, read other answers, or consult cited posts; score 0 if the answer is unintelligible without following references to other resources.
proposals.rationale: R02, R08, R39 are self-contained — dense_high. R13 says 'As shown in this post and in the accepted answer'; R31 builds entirely on 'mesel's answer' and another linked answer. Both dense_low with high card_pct.

proposals.name: Direct Interlocutor Address
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the text directly addresses the reader or asker using second-person pronouns and interactive questions (e.g., 'you did', 'can you think of'). Do not judge whether this is good or helpful.
proposals.rationale: The dense model reads end-to-end and seems sensitive to conversational register (R10, R20, R36), whereas the scorecard model rewards self-contained static answers.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Blunt Pedagogical Correction Tone
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the answer bluntly corrects the asker, points out errors, or uses a direct, authoritative tone (e.g., 'You mixed them up', 'Nope!'). Do not judge if the tone is appropriate.
proposals.rationale: Experienced users often authoritatively correct misconceptions (R12, R36, R50). This predicts dense model preference because it correlates with expertise, but tone itself is not a measure of mathematical quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: answerer's standing on the site

proposals.name: Heavy Mathematical Typography
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the answer relies on complex LaTeX display environments (e.g., \begin{align*}, matrices) and bold section headers. Do not judge if the formatting is good.
proposals.rationale: The scorecard model likely gives high marks to answers with heavy formal formatting (R22, R43, R26), but dense models may not weight formatting as heavily unless it reflects actual clarity.
proposals.upstream_parent: typographic and markup habit

proposals.name: External Citation Reliance
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the answer points to external sources (Wikipedia links, MathSciNet reviews, citations) instead of fully proving the result. Do not judge whether the citations are useful.
proposals.rationale: Experienced users often answer by citing literature or linking out (R06, R23, R34). This is predictive of dense scores due to high-expertise authors, but is not an intrinsic measure of standalone quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the format

proposals.name: Explicit Reference to Other Answers
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the text explicitly mentions other answers, other users, or previous comments in the thread. Do not judge if these references are helpful.
proposals.rationale: Later answers often explicitly position themselves relative to existing ones (R27, R44, R56). This marks the answer's position in the thread, affecting voter preference, but is not a measure of standalone quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream

proposals.name: Specific Engagement with Asker's Artifacts
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the answer explicitly quotes or evaluates the asker's specific work, formulations, or previous attempts (e.g., 'You got to here'). Do not judge if the evaluation is accurate.
proposals.rationale: Answers that directly debug the user's specific steps (R20, R46, R47) are highly valued by the dense model as they address the immediate problem, but are not generic mathematical criteria.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream

proposals.name: LLM-Style Templated Boilerplate
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the text uses generic, formulaic transitions typical of AI language models (e.g., 'To solve this problem, we can use...'). Do not judge the correctness or quality of the text.
proposals.rationale: The dense model may flag over-explained, low-density LLM-style text as lower quality compared to human answers (R04 and R14 exhibit this heavily).
proposals.upstream_parent: editing or assistance

proposals.name: Expert Terseness and Hint Provision
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the answer consists solely of a very brief hint, one-line formula, or terse nudge without providing the full derivation. Do not judge whether the hint is good.
proposals.rationale: High-reputation regulars often provide short, expert hints (R30, R39, R51). Voters often reward this expertise, while a rigid scorecard penalizes incompleteness.
proposals.upstream_parent: answerer's standing on the site

proposals.name: Authorial Hedging and Uncertainty
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the author admits uncertainty, corrects themselves, or explicitly notes possible errors in their own text (e.g., 'I'm not sure', 'Edit: this is broken'). Do not judge whether the admission is appropriate.
proposals.rationale: Human answers often contain live edits or uncertainty (R52, R55, R46), which a dense model might process neutrally, while a rigid scorecard heavily penalizes it.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission process dynamics

proposals.name: Self-Citation of Personal Work
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the author refers to their own books, lecture notes, colleagues, or personal prior posts. Do not judge the relevance of the self-citation.
proposals.rationale: Practised site regulars or academics naturally refer to their own materials (R19, R46). This predicts voter preference due to authority, but is a spurious channel for mathematical correctness.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's standing on the site
